clue.text: German ready to begin serving French prize?

parts.note: a tennis player standing on court is ready to begin serving

explanation.surface: A German stands poised to serve, perhaps hoping for some French award.
explanation.walkthrough: The Prix Goncourt is France's leading literary prize; the tennis picture of a server waiting supplies the bulk.
explanation.definitionFit: The Goncourt is the most famous annual literary award in France.

clue.text: Profit reported from good book

parts.note: a word sounding like profit is prophet, and the good book is the Bible, so this asks for a minor prophet with his own book there

explanation.walkthrough: Obadiah is the shortest book of the Old Testament, named after its prophet; 'Profit' stands in for the soundalike 'prophet'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament includes a short book named after this minor prophet.

clue.text: Mr Weller rises to hold up flickering light at Purification festival

indicators.note: in a down entry the first piece sits on top, holding up the piece below it

parts.note: a candle gives a flickering light

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means the name is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Sam Weller is Mr Pickwick's servant in Dickens's Pickwick Papers

explanation.surface: Dickens's Sam Weller lifts a guttering candle at a church feast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rises' reads the servant's name upwards as MAS, and 'to hold up' means the light sits on top of it in this down entry. Candlemas, 2 February, celebrates the Purification of the Virgin Mary.
explanation.definitionFit: Candlemas is the church feast marking the Purification of the Virgin and Christ's presentation in the Temple.

clue.text: New edition found at university by appointment

parts.note: being up means being in residence at university, especially Oxford or Cambridge
a date is an arranged appointment

explanation.surface: A fresh printing turns up in the college, released by arrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: An update is a revised version bringing a book or text up to the present.

clue.text: She thought Eliot modified 1927 work

indicators.note: modified tells us the letters of these three words are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman reckoned T. S. Eliot had revised a famous book from 1927.
explanation.walkthrough: 'modified' rearranges SHE THOUGHT ELIOT into Virginia Woolf's 1927 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Virginia Woolf's novel To the Lighthouse was published in 1927.

clue.text: Platform at church is for Ambrose

parts.note: a bier is the stand or platform on which a coffin rests
CE stands for Church of England

explanation.surface: A coffin stand in church is set aside for a man named Ambrose.
explanation.walkthrough: Ambrose Bierce was the American writer of The Devil's Dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrose is the first name of the American satirist Bierce.

clue.text: His illustrations are to be seen in Poets' Corner

definitions.text: His illustrations are to be seen in Poets' Corner

parts.words: His illustrations are to be seen in Poets' Corner
parts.note: Poets' Corner sounds like the Westminster Abbey memorial site, but here it is the title of a 1904 book of caricatures by an Edwardian wit

explanation.walkthrough: The Poets' Corner (1904) was Max Beerbohm's book of caricatures of writers, not the corner of Westminster Abbey.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Beerbohm drew the caricatures collected in the volume titled The Poets' Corner.

clue.text: That of Wyndham Lewis was written for love

definitions.text: That of Wyndham Lewis was written for love

parts.words: That of Wyndham Lewis was written for love
parts.note: Wyndham Lewis wrote a 1937 novel whose title is a word followed by 'for Love'

explanation.walkthrough: The novel is The Revenge for Love (1937); 'written for love' seems to mean done out of affection.
explanation.definitionFit: Wyndham Lewis's novel is titled The Revenge for Love, so this word precedes 'for Love'.

clue.text: People like Lamb first in attempts

indicators.note: in means the abbreviation for first is placed inside the word for attempts

parts.note: essays are attempts or tries
1st, written IST, is first

explanation.surface: Writers of Lamb's sort come top in their trials.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb wrote the Essays of Elia; 1ST is read as IST.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Lamb is among the best-known English writers of short prose pieces.

clue.text: Scott Fitzgerald's were beautiful also

parts.note: Fitzgerald's second novel is titled The Beautiful and ..., so the missing word describes them too

explanation.walkthrough: The novel is The Beautiful and Damned (1922).
explanation.definitionFit: Fitzgerald's 1922 novel is The Beautiful and Damned, so its people were cursed as well as lovely.

clue.text: Novel rollers possibly carrying us 5

parts.note: rollers are big sea breakers, which might carry us toward the title of 5 down; together this is another Woolf novel

explanation.walkthrough: Virginia Woolf wrote both 5 down and this 1931 novel; 'rollers' are ocean swells that could carry us to a lighthouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Virginia Woolf's 1931 novel takes its title from breakers on the sea.

clue.text: His early success was during the weekend

definitions.text: His early success was during the weekend

parts.words: His early success was during the weekend
parts.note: points to a writer whose first hit novel had Saturday Night and Sunday Morning as its title

explanation.walkthrough: Alan Sillitoe's first novel was Saturday Night and Sunday Morning (1958).
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Sillitoe made his name with Saturday Night and Sunday Morning, whose title spans a weekend.

clue.text: Woman writer conceals directions in early textile centre

indicators.note: conceals means the town's name wraps round and hides the compass points

parts.note: Bury in Lancashire was an early centre of cotton and wool manufacture
N and E, north and east, are compass directions

explanation.surface: A female author hides her bearings in an old mill town.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town in Lancashire, northern England, important in the early textile industry. Fanny Burney wrote Evelina.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Burney was an eighteenth-century English novelist and diarist.

clue.text: "I'm tired of love: I'm still more tired of —" (Belloc)

definitions.text: "I'm tired of love: I'm still more tired of —" (Belloc)

parts.words: "I'm tired of love: I'm still more tired of —" (Belloc)
parts.note: the missing word completes Belloc's couplet Fatigued, and must chime with the word that ends the second line

explanation.walkthrough: Belloc's lines run: I'm tired of Love: I'm still more tired of Rhyme. / But Money gives me pleasure all the time.
explanation.definitionFit: Belloc's verse Fatigued says he is weary of love and wearier still of versifying, with 'time' as the matching end word.

clue.text: Gypsy gentleman takes a French novel at the end of the day (with a whisky)

parts.note: roman is the French word for a novel

indicators.note: at the end of means we take only the last letter of the word day

parts.note: rye is a whisky distilled from rye grain

explanation.surface: A Romany gent picks up a novel from France at dusk, plus a dram.
explanation.walkthrough: In Romani, 'rye' means gentleman; George Borrow's 1857 novel is The Romany Rye.
explanation.definitionFit: In Romani speech, a rye is a gentleman, and a Romany one is a gentleman who lives among Gypsies, as in Borrow.

clue.text: Kundera's was insufferable

parts.note: Kundera's best-known novel speaks of the Unbearable ... of Being, and insufferable is a synonym for unbearable

explanation.walkthrough: Milan Kundera's novel is The Unbearable Lightness of Being (1984).
explanation.definitionFit: Kundera's novel title pairs this word with 'unbearable', a synonym of insufferable.

clue.text: A silly name could — one into nothing, thought Tristram Shandy

definitions.text: A silly name could — one into nothing, thought Tristram Shandy

parts.words: A silly name could — one into nothing, thought Tristram Shandy
parts.note: in Sterne's novel the Shandy view of names is that a foolish one could '...' a child into nothing, a name used as a verb

explanation.walkthrough: In Tristram Shandy, Walter Shandy holds that a name shapes character: some names could Nicodemus a man into nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterne's Walter Shandy cites the biblical Pharisee's name as one that would doom a boy to insignificance.

clue.text: Negligent, like V. S. Pritchett's widow

definitions.meaning: Pritchett wrote a short story titled The ... Widow

explanation.walkthrough: V. S. Pritchett's story The Careless Widow (1981) gives the second sense; 'widow' is not his real wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Negligent means heedless, and Pritchett's story is called The Careless Widow.

clue.text: Cameo thus devised to adorn Amis's biographer

indicators.note: devised means the letters are worked out anew, rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: A carved brooch, newly designed, is meant to decorate the man who wrote Amis's life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devised' rearranges CAMEO THUS. The definition is something worn on the upper lip, read loosely as decoration for a man's face.
explanation.definitionFit: Facial hair on the upper lip is a traditional adornment of a man's face.

clue.text: Many among Spanish ones suggest philosopher

indicators.note: among means the letter for many goes in between the two Spanish words

parts.note: una and uno are the feminine and masculine Spanish words for one
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so many

explanation.surface: Plenty of Spaniards hint at a thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' sets the thousand inside the pair of Spanish words. Miguel de Unamuno (1864-1936) was a Basque-born philosopher, novelist and rector of Salamanca.
explanation.definitionFit: Miguel de Unamuno was a Spanish thinker, author of The Tragic Sense of Life.

clue.text: Language from South Beds.

parts.note: cots are small beds

explanation.surface: A tongue spoken in southern Bedfordshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beds.' looks like the abbreviation for Bedfordshire, an English county; it is just beds.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots is the Germanic tongue of Lowland Scotland.

clue.text: Hilton's Catherine Herself may have described this sort of artisan

indicators.note: sort of signals a version of the word artisan with its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: James Hilton's novel heroine might have been a kind of craftswoman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges ARTISAN. James Hilton's first novel was Catherine Herself (1920); the title suggests Catherine the Great.
explanation.definitionFit: A Catherine in her own right suggests the Russian empress, an imperial consort and ruler.

clue.text: Vibration, of design from Burgess

definitions.meaning: Anthony Burgess wrote ... of Intent, and intent means design

explanation.walkthrough: Burgess's 1966 spy novel is Tremor of Intent; 'of design' paraphrases 'of Intent'.
explanation.definitionFit: A quiver or shake is a vibration, and Burgess's novel title gives this word before 'of Intent'.

clue.text: French distinction

parts.note: a fine shade of difference, using a word borrowed from French

explanation.walkthrough: 'French distinction' suggests an honour like the Legion of Honour, but it is a subtle difference, a word taken from French.
explanation.definitionFit: A subtle shade of meaning, a word borrowed from French, is a fine distinction.

clue.text: Leading man said to turn round and play the queen in Salomeé

parts.note: a hero is the leading man of a story

indicators.note: to turn round means the word said is read backwards

explanation.surface: The star actor is said to swing round and take the part of the queen in Wilde's play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn round' gives DIAS. Herodias is Herod's wife and Salome's mother in Oscar Wilde's play; the printed 'Salomeé' is an OCR slip for Salomé.
explanation.definitionFit: In Wilde's Salomé, Herod's wife is Salome's mother and the royal consort.

clue.text: Artist well acquainted with French customs

definitions.text: Artist well acquainted with French customs

parts.words: Artist well acquainted with French customs
parts.note: the painter nicknamed Le Douanier worked as a customs official in Paris, so knew French customs from the inside

explanation.walkthrough: Henri Rousseau was called Le Douanier (the customs man) from his job at the Paris toll office; 'customs' seems to mean habits.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Rousseau, the naive painter, was a French toll and customs officer before painting full time.

clue.text: Souvenir of Rome I'm rewriting

indicators.note: rewriting means the letters of these two words are set down in a new order

explanation.surface: A keepsake of Rome, as I redraft my account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewriting' rearranges ROME and I'M; French souvenir means memory or remembrance.
explanation.definitionFit: A souvenir in the sense of a written remembrance is a recollection of one's life.

clue.text: This success for Uris is way-out

definitions.text: This success for Uris is way-out

parts.words: This success for Uris is way-out
parts.note: Leon Uris's 1958 bestseller has a Greek title literally meaning a road out

explanation.walkthrough: Leon Uris's bestseller Exodus (1958); the Greek ex hodos means way out, while 'way-out' seems to mean bizarre.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek word behind Uris's title combines out and road, a departure or exit.

clue.text: Deserve Irish dramatist: get Bronte family

parts.note: to earn something is to deserve it
George Bernard Shaw was an Irish playwright

explanation.surface: Merit an Irish playwright and you receive the Brontes' relations.
explanation.walkthrough: The Earnshaws are a family in Emily Bronte's Wuthering Heights.
explanation.definitionFit: Catherine and Hindley belong to the household at Wuthering Heights in Emily Bronte's novel.
